title: Tiny GPU FPGA Port — Sipeed Tang Nano 20K
description: Porting a custom 32-bit SIMT GPU from simulation onto a Gowin GW2AR-18C FPGA: a resource-driven redesign from 4 cores × 4 threads down to 1 × 1 with sequential block execution, plus a hardware top level with clock, memory init, launch FSM and UART readback.
status: Build flow complete — bring-up paused while compiler work continues
overview:
This is the FPGA arm of the 32-Bit Tiny GPU project: taking a design that was written for simulation and an ASIC flow, and making it fit and run on a real, small, cheap FPGA.

The target is a Sipeed Tang Nano 20K — a Gowin GW2AR-18C QN88 with a 27 MHz onboard oscillator. That board has far fewer LUTs, registers and routing resources than the simulation configuration assumes, so the port is not a recompile. The design drops from 4 cores × 4 threads executing in parallel to a single core with a single thread executing four blocks sequentially, which trades throughput for fit while keeping the programming model and the ISA identical.

Around the GPU core sits a hardware top level that does the things a testbench used to do for free: bring up the clock, initialise program and data memory from hex images, drive a launch FSM to start execution, light status LEDs, and stream results back over UART so the board can be observed without a debugger.

The port is a separate concern from the ASIC flow — the same RTL also goes through OpenLane to a signoff-clean GDSII on SkyWater 130 nm.
objectives: Fit a design written for 4 cores × 4 threads onto a resource-constrained Gowin GW2AR-18C
Preserve the ISA and programming model while changing the execution configuration
Build a synthesis-ready flattened Verilog view of a SystemVerilog design for toolchain compatibility
Write an FPGA top level handling clock, memory initialisation, launch sequencing, LEDs and UART
Produce pin constraints and a repeatable build flow through Gowin EDA to a flashed board
Get observable output off the hardware over UART rather than inferring behaviour

challenges.title: The simulation configuration does not fit
challenges.description: The full design runs 4 cores with 4 threads each. The Tang Nano 20K's LUT, register and routing budget cannot hold that, and simply reducing parameters risks changing what the kernels mean.
challenges.solution: Reconfigured to a single core with a single thread and moved to sequential execution of four blocks. Throughput drops, but the ISA, kernel binaries and programming model stay identical, so a kernel verified in simulation is the same kernel on the board.

challenges.title: Toolchain SystemVerilog support
challenges.description: The RTL is written in SystemVerilog with parameterised modules, but vendor FPGA flows vary in how much of the language they accept — and a synthesis failure deep in a vendor tool is far less legible than a simulator error.
challenges.solution: Generated gpu_combined.v, a flattened synthesis-ready Verilog view of the design, so the FPGA flow consumes a form the toolchain handles reliably while simulation keeps using the full SystemVerilog source.

challenges.title: A testbench provides everything real hardware does not
challenges.description: In simulation, memory is preloaded, execution is kicked off by the testbench, and results are read straight out of signals. On a board none of that exists — the design has to initialise itself and expose its own results.
challenges.solution: Wrote an FPGA top level that loads program and data memory from hex images, sequences kernel launch through an FSM, drives status LEDs, and streams results over UART so behaviour is observable without a debugger attached.

results: Complete documented build flow from AXEL kernel hex through Gowin EDA synthesis, place and route, bitstream and flashing
Single-core, single-thread configuration executing four blocks sequentially, fitting the Gowin GW2AR-18C resource budget
Flattened synthesis-ready gpu_combined.v generated from the SystemVerilog source for toolchain compatibility
FPGA top level handling clock, program and data memory initialisation, launch FSM, status LEDs and UART output
Tang Nano 20K pin constraints file mapping clock, LEDs and UART
Post-synthesis timing reported as acceptable for the board's 27 MHz clock
Same RTL also taken through OpenLane to a signoff-clean GDSII on SkyWater 130 nm — two independent implementation paths from one source
futureWork: Finish on-board bring-up — the port is paused while compiler and kernel work takes priority
Push the configuration back up toward multiple threads per core as resource use is trimmed
Add on-board performance counters so measured cycle counts can be compared against simulation
Explore a larger FPGA to run the full 4 × 4 parallel configuration
